chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Saeed, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Asim ibn Humayd, from Abu Baseer, who said:

I said to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him): 'An old man from our companions, called Umar, asked Isa ibn A'yan while he was needy. Isa ibn A'yan said to him: 'Indeed, I have some zakat with me, but I will not give you from it.' He said to him: 'And why?' He said: 'Because I saw you buying meat and dates.' He said: 'I only profited by a dirham, so I bought meat with two dinars (or coins), and dates with two dinars (or coins), then I returned with two dinars (or coins) for a need.'

He said: So Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) placed his hand on his forehead for a while, then raised his head, then said: 'Indeed, Allah, Blessed and High, looked at the wealth of the rich, then looked at the poor, and made in the wealth of the rich that which suffices them. And if it did not suffice them, He would have increased it for them. Rather, he should give him what he eats, drinks, wears, marries with, gives in charity, and performs Hajj with.'

key_terms.عِيسَى بْنَ أَعْيَن: Isa ibn A'yan (a companion known for his piety)

ai.seo_question: What is the proper scope of needs covered by zakat according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) uses this incident to refute the restrictive view that zakat is merely for immediate survival, establishing instead that it serves as a comprehensive means of financial independence (istighna) for the recipient. This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly principle that zakat should enable the poor to meet all essential life expenses—including marriage and Hajj—thereby elevating their social and economic status rather than keeping them in perpetual dependency.
